summary: A humorous, satirical incident report on a windstorm that knocked out the power grid and cell network in autumn 2023. It follows quotes from residents and officials as people cope with the outage through campfires, matches, conversation and makeshift lawn campsites, while engineers mount a restoration effort. The piece ends on a cliffhanger as communities wait for the lights to return.
one_line: A tongue-in-cheek account of a September 2023 windstorm blackout, with residents' quips, the loss of power and cell service, and a cliffhanger awaiting restoration.
key_facts: The windstorm began on a chilly morning on September 15, 2023, and disrupted the electrical grid.
Steve McCrank, a local wind watcher, joked that leaves teamed up with the wind and played tick-tack-toe on the power lines.
The piece refers to September 20th as the day a 'symphony of electrical impedance' spread across the nation.
Janet Gridley, spokesperson for the energy provider, said "We've built this city on rock and roll, but maybe we should've considered some sturdier stuff."
The outage is dubbed 'The Great Offline Epoch of September 27th', during which families gathered around campfires and children marveled at paperback books.
Gregg Hapsburg, father of two TikTokkers, said the Wi-Fi outage let his family rediscover 'the ancient art of conversation'.
Toppled antennae left the telecommunications network down, and citizens climbed hills searching for a single signal bar.
Barbara Linksys said the only bars she found on her hilltop climb were those advertising 'Happy Hour'.
Tom Flint said he had practiced fire-making since watching a survival show last year and made local headlines for using matches during the blackout.
Engineers launched 'The Power Surge Revival Tour', and Martha Volt, who knew a breaker box better than her kitchen pantry, became an overnight sensation.
The outage lasted approximately one week, turning suburban lawns into makeshift campsites with grills, bonfires and tents.
Larry and Linda Lawnchair pitched a tent they last used in '98; the article calls them pioneers of yard utility.
The article ends with families gathered by oil lamps, awaiting a possible restoration of power, in a cliffhanger.
